terms.def: The unused floor area permitted on a zoning lot beyond what is already built. In some circumstances, those unused development rights may be transferred to another lot — often to allow a neighboring property to build larger than its own zoning would otherwise permit.

A proposal that complies with all applicable zoning rules and does not require discretionary approval from the City Planning Commission or Board of Standards and Appeals. As-of-right projects can proceed directly to a building permit without community board or public review.

A discretionary action by the City Planning Commission that modifies specified zoning requirements when required findings are met. Less involved than a special permit, and does not require a full ULURP vote by the City Council.
The maximum permitted height of a building's street wall before any required setback. Once a building reaches its base height, it must step back from the street before continuing upward.

The size and shape of a building as controlled by zoning regulations — including lot size, floor area ratio (FAR), lot coverage, open space, yards, height, and setback requirements. Bulk regulations determine how large and in what form a building can be built.
A C1 or C2 district mapped within a residential zoning district to allow neighborhood-serving retail and related commercial uses on ground floors. Common in areas like Park Slope and Carroll Gardens.

The primary zoning control for building size: total building floor area divided by the area of the zoning lot. A FAR of 2.0 on a 5,000 sq ft lot allows up to 10,000 sq ft of floor area. Higher FAR = larger buildings permitted.

A recorded legal covenant that binds current and future property owners to specific conditions, mitigation requirements, environmental remediation, or other obligations tied to a project approval. It runs with the land.

A discretionary approval that allows modification of use, bulk, or parking rules when specific findings are met. Some special permits go through the City Planning Commission via ULURP; others go to the BSA. CB6 reviews and votes on CPC special permits.

Relief from zoning rules granted where strict compliance would create practical difficulty or hardship. For area variances (bulk), all five findings under ZR §72-21 must be proven. Granted by the Board of Standards and Appeals, not the CPC.

The system of district-based rules that regulates land use and development across New York City. Zoning determines what can be built, how large, and for what purpose on any given lot. The NYC Zoning Resolution has been in place since 1961, built on the foundation of the 1916 resolution.

The unit of land to which zoning regulations apply. A zoning lot may consist of one or more tax lots. FAR, coverage, and other bulk controls are calculated based on the zoning lot, not individual tax lots.

A change to the text of the NYC Zoning Resolution itself — as opposed to a map change. Text amendments can apply citywide or be limited to specific areas. They go through ULURP and require City Council approval.
A change to the official NYC Zoning Map — changing a district's boundaries or classification. Commonly called a rezoning. Goes through ULURP and requires City Council approval.

Short for Special Purpose District. A zoning layer that the City Planning Commission maps over the underlying districts to achieve specific planning and urban-design goals in a defined area. Its rules modify, supplement, or override the base zoning, and where they conflict the special-district rules control. On the city zoning map these appear as a special district code. The one mapped in CB6 is the Special Gowanus Mixed Use District (code G).

The special purpose district created by the 2021 Gowanus rezoning. It pairs residential and light-manufacturing (M1) districts so housing and industry can sit side by side, and is organized into five subdistricts with their own rules. It layers Mandatory Inclusionary Housing onto mapped areas, treats blocks along the Gowanus Canal as waterfront subject to a Waterfront Access Plan, and adds environmental, ground-floor, and streetscape requirements on top of the base zoning. Found in the NYC Zoning Resolution, Article XIII, Chapter 9.

The NYC Zoning Resolution organizes permitted uses into numbered groups (UG 1 through UG 18). Each zoning district permits certain use groups. For example, residential districts permit UG 1–4; manufacturing districts permit UGs up to 18.

City Environmental Quality Review — New York City's environmental review process for discretionary actions, implementing SEQRA at the city level. CEQR assesses whether a proposed action may have significant adverse environmental impacts in areas including land use, traffic, noise, air quality, and historic resources.

New York State Environmental Quality Review Act — state law requiring all government agencies to assess environmental impacts of discretionary actions before approving them. CEQR is New York City's local implementation. Applies to rezonings, special permits, and other discretionary approvals.

A standardized form used under SEQR/CEQR to assess whether a proposed action may have significant environmental impacts. Applicants complete Part 1; the lead agency completes Parts 2 and 3. The EAF determines whether a full Environmental Impact Statement is required.

A detailed study of a proposed action's potential environmental impacts, required when a lead agency issues a Positive Declaration under SEQR/CEQR. Includes a draft EIS (public comment period), scoping, and final EIS. CB6 can participate in scoping and comment on the draft.

A formal determination that a proposed action will not have a significant adverse impact on the environment. A Negative Declaration means no Environmental Impact Statement is required and the project can move forward through other approvals.
A formal determination that a proposed action may have significant adverse environmental impacts. A Positive Declaration triggers the requirement for a full Environmental Impact Statement (EIS).

A SEQR determination that a proposed action would have environmental impacts, but that enforceable conditions imposed on the project can reduce those impacts to a level below significance. Less common than a straight Negative Declaration.

The government agency designated to coordinate the SEQR/CEQR environmental review when multiple agencies have approval authority over an action. The lead agency conducts the EAF review, makes the significance determination, and, if required, oversees the EIS process.

The process by which the lead agency and the public define the range of issues and alternatives to be studied in a Draft EIS. CB6 can participate in scoping to ensure relevant neighborhood concerns — like flooding, traffic, or historic resources — are included.

Approval from the Landmarks Preservation Commission that proposed exterior work on a landmarked building or property within a historic district is appropriate to the character of the landmark. CB6's Landmarks & Land Use Committee reviews CoA applications and submits an advisory recommendation before the LPC public hearing.

The city agency responsible for designating and regulating landmarks and historic districts in New York City. LPC designates individual landmarks, interior landmarks, scenic landmarks, and historic districts. CB6 has 6 historic districts within its boundaries.

A defined area designated by the LPC for its architectural, cultural, or historic significance. Exterior changes to buildings within a historic district generally require a Certificate of Appropriateness from LPC. In CB6, major historic districts include Park Slope, Cobble Hill, Carroll Gardens, and Boerum Hill.

An LPC approval for minor work on a landmarked property or within a historic district that has no effect on the protected architectural features. Less involved than a full Certificate of Appropriateness.

A finding that the cost of LPC-compliant preservation would make a property economically undevelopable. An owner can apply for a hardship determination from LPC, which may allow modifications to otherwise required preservation standards.

The ability to transfer unused development rights from a landmark site to a receiving lot. TDRs are commonly used to compensate landmark owners who cannot build to their full FAR while allowing a neighboring site to build larger. Requires LPC and CPC approval.

The Uniform Land Use Review Procedure — the city's formal public review process for major land use actions including rezonings, special permits, acquisitions, dispositions, and city map changes. ULURP gives CB6 a 60-day window to hold a public hearing and issue an advisory recommendation.

An action that requires a government agency to make a judgment-based decision — as opposed to ministerial or as-of-right approvals. Discretionary actions typically require ULURP, SEQR/CEQR review, or both. CB6 reviews discretionary actions within its boundaries.

The period before a ULURP application is officially certified by DCP and the public review clock starts. DCP may require community engagement, environmental review, or other steps during pre-certification. CB6 often engages with applicants during this phase.

See ULURP. The formal public review sequence: Community Board (60 days) → Borough President (30 days) → City Planning Commission (60 days) → City Council (50 days) → Mayor (5 days). CB6's vote is advisory but part of the official record.

Specific criteria that an agency must affirmatively determine before granting a discretionary approval. For example, all five BSA variance findings under ZR §72-21 must be met. If required findings cannot be made, approval must be denied.

A city program, adopted in 2016, that requires a percentage of units in newly-rezoned areas to be permanently affordable. Several options exist, including 25% of units at 60% AMI or 30% at 80% AMI. MIH applies to all rezonings that allow residential use.

The midpoint of a region's income distribution, set annually by HUD for the New York metro area. Affordable housing programs set rents or sale prices as a percentage of AMI. 100% AMI for a family of four in NYC is roughly $130,000.

Housing where costs (rent or purchase price) are restricted based on income. Generally defined as costing no more than 30% of a household's gross income. NYC uses AMI thresholds to define affordability levels across different programs.

A property tax exemption program for new residential construction tied to affordability requirements. Originally created in 1971. Expired in June 2022. Successor legislation has been debated but not enacted as of 2025.

NYC's official platform for affordable housing lottery applications. Residents can apply for income-restricted units across the city. CB6's Rental Rankings & Housing tab includes direct links to active lotteries.

New York City Housing Authority — the city agency that owns and manages public housing developments. CB6 includes two NYCHA developments: Gowanus Houses (1,134 units) and Wyckoff Gardens (528 units). Both were central to the Gowanus rezoning negotiations.
